newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania minister resigns in corruption scandal.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania minister resigns in corruption scandal.

text.p: Tanzanian Finance Minister Simon Mbilinyi has resigned after months of speculation over his role in an import tax scandal that cast a shadow over President Benjamin Mkapa's crackdown on corruption.
Mkapa's press secretary Patrick Chokala, said Mbilinyi resigned on Sunday "to allow state organs to investigate allegations of corruption against him and other officials".

"The president has appointed Daniel Yona as acting finance minister. Mbilinyi said he resigned to strengthen (the ruling) CCM party and the government," Chokala said in a statement issued in the inland city of Dodoma on Monday.
Mkapa had put stamping out corruption at the top of his agenda when he campaigned for the presidency in October 1995.
Mbilinyi's resignation comes on the eve of an international investment forum in Dar es Salaam which aims to promote Tanzania as a stable base in East Africa for foreign investment.
The ruling CCM party has been riven by bitter wrangling over the past few weeks on whether Mbilinyi should step down on allegations about his role in a tax exemption scandal.
Daniel Yona, an economist, is currently minister of state for planning. He formerly worked at the Bank of Tanzania.
A parliament probe report published in September said Mbilinyi, an economics professor, acted improperly over the importation of cooking oil and should be "taken to task".
The report said Mbilinyi ignored advice from his ministry officials who said the oil should not be exempt from tax.
"Circumstantial evidence suggests that there was a motive that drove the minister to act against advice," said House Speaker Pius Msekwa, who chaired the parliament committee.

The chairman of the main opposition party, Augustine Mrema, has accused senior Tanzanian ministers and officials of accepting 900 million Tanzanian shillings (around $1.5 million) in bribes to facilitate the tax waiver.

The tax exemptions were given to four local companies and covered a shipment of 4,700 tonnes of cooking oil. Importers were allowed to pay import duty at a concessional rate well below the amount stipulated in government statutes.

A similar import tax exemption scandal discovered by the World Bank in 1994 led to the downfall of then finance minister Kighoma Malima and a suspension of $200 million in donor balance of payments support.
Msekwa's committee said Mbilinyi also acted improperly in sanctioning the reduction in the price of export fish fillets from Lake Victoria, a decision that gave traders a more favourable tax rate.
The committee said: "Evidence has shown that normal procedures were flouted and expert advice was ignored."

In a speech on corruption last week, Trade Minister Abdallah Kigoda suggested a tough line against Mbilinyi. "It's a very importanty question. Our government has said openly that one of its biggest challenges is to fight corruption. It must."
